problem: Hierarchical VLN planners (DUET, BEVBert) recover from mistakes with late-fused global/local scores over a cluttered graph memory that treats all viewpoints equally, ignoring novelty, recency and instruction alignment of frontiers. Progress-monitoring methods regress a sparse distance-to-goal signal that is hard to estimate in unseen environments.
motivation: Error recovery is essential for long-horizon instruction following in partially observed environments. Humans back-track to the most promising recent alternative, and curiosity-style novelty seeking helps object search but must be constrained by instruction agreement in VLN.
key_idea: Predict a per-candidate recovery-confidence score, and when all candidates are low, jump to the frontier ranked highest by action score, recency, novelty and DTW-based instruction-entity alignment kept in an action memory and a scene-object memory.
insight: Recovery benefits from choosing frontiers that are recent, novel and instruction-aligned, rather than a generic back-track. The kidnapping perturbation study shows the smallest SR drops among memory types (e.g. -13/-17 on 'Close' vs -18/-21 for BEVBert). Gains over the BEVBert baseline are modest (+2.6 SR on R2R test unseen), and the paper does not report per-component ablations of the scoring terms.
method: Action memory: directed graph of visited/frontier nodes with observation time step and edges holding action scores from the planner; edges between visited nodes are zeroed to prevent re-visits.
Scene-object memory: per-viewpoint knowledge vector as sum of ViCo embeddings of top-K Faster R-CNN (Visual Genome) objects; added to memory only if the novelty score exceeds 2.

Recovery confidence: sigmoid FFN on local cell-instruction embedding C_t predicts per-candidate confidence, trained online with MSE against 1 - normalised distance to the nearest GT path node. Exploration is triggered when all candidates fall below c_thresh.

Frontier scoring: S = S_act * S_recency * (S_novel + S_align). S_act sums incident edge scores, S_recency = exp(gamma(t_i - t)) with gamma=0.1, S_novel is the inverse cosine similarity to memory, and S_align is the FastDTW cost between instruction entity embeddings and the knowledge sequence of the test path. Only frontiers with S_act > 0.5 are scored; the agent takes the shortest path to the argmax.
Deviation prediction pretraining: an auxiliary task classifies path steps as on-track/deviated/recovering on synthetic perturbed R2R paths, mixed with MLM, SAP, MRC and OG.
Base planner: BEVBert-style dual-scale planner (global topological CMT + local BEV map CMT with fused action scores), trained by imitation learning with loss weight lambda=0.4.

setting.backbone: BEVBert-based dual-scale cross-modal transformers (trained), Faster R-CNN (VG) object detector, ViCo embeddings
setting.training_data: R2R (with synthetic perturbed paths for deviation prediction) and R4R; pretraining tasks MLM, SAP, MRC, OG, DP; imitation learning
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views), panoramic depth, poses
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints, with shortest-path jumps to frontiers
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT path used only in training for confidence and deviation labels)

numbers_note: The R4R text says ValUnseen SR is 35%, but Table 2 prints 38; the table value is used.
results: StratXplore reaches R2R val-unseen SR 77.61 / SPL 66.92 and test-unseen SR 75.86 / SPL 64.79, beating the BEVBert baseline (75/64 val-unseen, 73/62 test) and DUET. On R4R it obtains the best SR (66 val-seen, 38 val-unseen) and CLS versus SSM, but nDTW/SDTW are not better and trajectories are longer.
limitations: Frontier comparison happens post-facto in a separate recovery module, adding ranking cost, rather than being integrated into the planner.
Path correction lengthens trajectories and lowers nDTW/SDTW on R4R.
Improvements over BEVBert are modest, and no per-component ablation is reported.
